set.stem: A 36-year-old woman rescued from a house fire remains obtunded, with seizures, hypotension and a bitter almond odour on her breath. Which test will confirm the diagnosis?
set.explanation: Burning plastics and wool release hydrogen cyanide, which blocks cytochrome oxidase; coma, seizures, shock and a bitter almond odour in a smoke-inhalation victim suggest cyanide toxicity, confirmed by the red cell cyanide concentration. Because that result is slow, a lactate above about 8 mmol/L is used as a supportive marker and treatment (hydroxocobalamin with 100% oxygen) should not wait for it. Carboxyhaemoglobin must also be measured in any fire victim, but CO poisoning does not cause the almond odour, and ammonia and methaemoglobin are not the relevant tests.

set.stem: A 28-year-old has recurrent sinus and lung infections and cystic fibrosis is suspected. Which finding best confirms the diagnosis?
set.explanation: A sweat chloride of 60 mmol/L or more on two occasions (with a compatible clinical picture) confirms cystic fibrosis; 30–59 mmol/L is intermediate and needs CFTR genotyping or nasal potential difference testing. A single F508del allele is only carrier status unless a second disease-causing mutation is found, and CF gives an increased (more negative), not decreased, nasal potential difference. Pseudomonas in sputum is supportive but occurs in other forms of bronchiectasis.

set.stem: A 42-year-old man has progressive dyspnoea and weight loss. Bronchoalveolar lavage returns milky fluid containing PAS-positive material. What is the diagnosis?
set.explanation: Milky, opaque lavage fluid with PAS-positive lipoproteinaceous material is diagnostic of pulmonary alveolar proteinosis, which in adults is usually autoimmune (anti-GM-CSF antibodies impair macrophage clearance of surfactant). HRCT shows 'crazy-paving' ground-glass change with septal thickening. Pneumocystis also produces foamy PAS-positive exudate but occurs in immunosuppressed patients and shows cysts on silver stain, while DIP, organising pneumonia and nocardiosis do not give milky lavage. Nocardia infection is a recognised complication of PAP.

set.stem: A patient has symptomatic pulmonary alveolar proteinosis with hypoxaemia. What is the most appropriate treatment?
set.explanation: Whole-lung lavage under general anaesthesia, washing each lung in turn with saline through a double-lumen tube, physically removes the accumulated surfactant and remains the standard treatment for symptomatic PAP. Inhaled GM-CSF (molgramostim) is an effective newer option for autoimmune PAP. Corticosteroids and cytotoxics do not help and increase the risk of infection, and antibiotics are only for proven superinfection such as nocardiosis.

set.stem: A 52-year-old man has obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Which statement is true?
options: Mutation of the PHOX2B gene is associated with this condition
CPAP alone is always adequate therapy
Intubation is mandatory for acute hypercapnia
Coexistent obstructive sleep apnoea occurs in only 25% of cases
Weight loss will lead to improvements in PaCO2 over time
set.explanation: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome is daytime hypercapnia (PaCO2 >6 kPa, 45 mmHg) in an obese person (BMI ≥30 kg/m²) without another cause, and sustained weight loss (including after bariatric surgery) improves PaCO2 and oxygenation. About 90% also have obstructive sleep apnoea; CPAP is enough for many, but those with persistent hypoventilation need bilevel NIV, and acute hypercapnic decompensation is usually managed with NIV rather than intubation. PHOX2B mutations cause congenital central hypoventilation syndrome.

set.stem: A 52-year-old man with loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas, daytime sleepiness and a high BMI is thought to have obstructive sleep apnoea. He has no significant cardiopulmonary or neuromuscular disease and no symptoms of another sleep disorder. What is the most appropriate next step?
set.explanation: In an uncomplicated adult with a high pre-test probability of moderate-to-severe OSA, a validated home (limited-channel) sleep apnoea test is an accurate and cost-effective first diagnostic step; in-laboratory polysomnography is reserved for those with significant comorbidity, suspected other sleep disorders, or a negative or inconclusive home study. Oximetry alone can miss events, CPAP should not be started without an objective diagnosis, and surgery is not first-line in adults.

why: Added the absence of comorbidity/other sleep disorders so home testing is the single best answer over in-lab polysomnography

set.stem: A 48-year-old man with moderate obstructive sleep apnoea refuses CPAP. Which statement about untreated obstructive sleep apnoea is correct?
options: It has no significant effect on mortality
It is not associated with depression
It increases the risk of motor vehicle accidents
It has no effect on blood pressure
Its complications are prevented by sleeping with extra pillows
set.explanation: Untreated OSA causes daytime sleepiness and roughly doubles to triples the risk of road traffic accidents, and patients with excessive sleepiness must be advised not to drive until treated (and to inform the licensing authority where required). It is also associated with hypertension (often resistant), atrial fibrillation, stroke, increased cardiovascular mortality and depression, so the other statements are false. CPAP improves sleepiness, accident risk and blood pressure.

why: Original options were all false negations with 'All of the above' as answer; rewritten so one statement is correct

set.stem: The polysomnogram shown demonstrates a waxing and waning (crescendo–decrescendo) breathing pattern with central apnoeas. Which patient is most likely to have this pattern?
options: A 6-year-old with enlarged tonsils and adenoids
A 48-year-old obese man with loud snoring
A 52-year-old menopausal woman with frequent awakenings
A 68-year-old with atrial fibrillation and ischaemic cardiomyopathy (EF 15%), raised JVP and oedema
set.explanation: Cheyne–Stokes respiration, cyclical crescendo–decrescendo breathing separated by central apnoeas (no flow and no chest or abdominal effort), is typical of advanced heart failure, where prolonged circulation time and an exaggerated ventilatory response to CO2 destabilise breathing. Opioids such as methadone also cause central apnoea, but with an irregular (ataxic) pattern rather than the smooth waxing and waning shown. Enlarged tonsils and obesity cause obstructive apnoea with continued respiratory effort. Treatment is optimisation of heart failure therapy.

why: Same idea and level as resx-0071 (CPAP is the most effective treatment for moderate–severe OSA)

set.stem: A 25-year-old with cystic fibrosis is referred for lung transplantation. What is the main impediment to long-term survival after transplantation?
set.explanation: Chronic lung allograft dysfunction, mainly bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (progressive obstructive loss of FEV1 from fibrotic small-airway obliteration), affects about half of recipients by 5 years and is the principal cause of late death, limiting median survival to about 6–7 years. Primary graft dysfunction causes early deaths, CMV infection is mostly an early problem controlled by prophylaxis, and PTLD and chronic kidney disease (from calcineurin inhibitors) are important but less frequent causes of mortality.

set.stem: A 42-year-old man in haemorrhagic shock has a lactate of 4.8 mmol/L. Which factor is least important in determining oxygen delivery to his tissues?
set.explanation: Oxygen delivery equals cardiac output × arterial oxygen content, and content = (1.34 × Hb × SaO2) + (0.023 × PaO2 in kPa); dissolved oxygen is tiny, so PaO2 matters mainly through its effect on saturation. Improving cardiac output (volume) and haemoglobin (blood transfusion) has by far the largest effect in haemorrhagic shock, whereas raising PaO2 above the level giving full saturation adds little. The rising lactate reflects inadequate delivery to tissues.

set.stem: A 67-year-old woman is intubated for pneumonia on a background of COPD. All of the following are measures that prevent ICU complications EXCEPT:
set.explanation: Intensive insulin therapy aiming for normoglycaemia (4.4–6.1 mmol/L) increased mortality and severe hypoglycaemia in NICE-SUGAR, so a target of about 8–10 mmol/L is recommended. VTE prophylaxis with LMWH, stress-ulcer prophylaxis in ventilated patients, early mobilisation to limit ICU-acquired weakness and central line bundles to prevent bloodstream infection are all established preventive measures. Head-of-bed elevation and daily sedation holds also reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia.

In shock, hypotension reduces baroreceptor firing, which disinhibits the vasomotor centre and increases sympathetic (adrenergic) output and catecholamine release to support pressure, so the statement that hypotension inhibits it is false. The other statements are true: the stress response raises cortisol and catecholamines, which increase gluconeogenesis and lipolysis; hyperglycaemia and metabolites raise extracellular osmolality and draw fluid from cells; mitochondrial dysfunction leads to anaerobic metabolism and lactate accumulation; and inflammatory mediators drive multiorgan failure.

set.stem: A patient with a C2–3 spinal cord transection is in shock. Which haemodynamic profile is expected?
options: Low CO, high SVR, low RA pressure, low PCWP, low SvO2
Low CO, high SVR, high RA pressure, high PCWP, low SvO2
High CO, low SVR, low RA pressure, low PCWP, high SvO2
Low CO, normal SVR, high RA pressure, low PCWP, low SvO2
Low CO, low SVR, low RA pressure, low PCWP, low SvO2
set.explanation: A high cervical cord transection interrupts sympathetic outflow, causing arterial and venous dilatation (low SVR, pooling with low RA pressure and PCWP) and unopposed vagal tone with bradycardia, so cardiac output falls and tissue oxygen extraction rises, lowering SvO2. Hypovolaemic shock gives low filling pressures with a high SVR, cardiogenic shock gives high filling pressures with a high SVR, and early septic shock is hyperdynamic. Treatment is fluids, vasopressors and atropine or pacing for bradycardia.

why: Removed attached table image whose rows did not match the text options; option E reordered for clarity (content unchanged)

set.explanation: In large international ICU surveys (EPIC II/III) Gram-negative organisms remain the most frequently isolated cause of sepsis (about 60% of positive cultures), with Gram-positive bacteria second, so the statement that Gram-positive organisms predominate is the false one. The other statements are accurate: respiratory infection is the commonest source, most patients have significant comorbidity, blood cultures are positive in roughly 40–70% of septic shock, and the recorded incidence has been rising with an ageing, more immunosuppressed population.

why: Parse fragment: the first half of Harrison Q43 (sepsis classification); the complete question is resx-0052

set.stem: A 62-year-old man with right lower lobe pneumonia is confused, with RR 28/min, HR 118/min and BP 84/50 mmHg, which rises to 112/70 mmHg after 2 L of IV crystalloid without vasopressors. ABG on air: pH 7.46, PaCO2 4.3 kPa (32 mmHg), PaO2 10.1 kPa (76 mmHg); lactate 1.6 mmol/L. How should his condition be classified?
options: Systemic inflammatory response syndrome without infection
set.explanation: Under Sepsis-3, sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction (SOFA rise ≥2) caused by a dysregulated response to infection; this man has pneumonia with confusion and hypotension, meeting that definition. Septic shock additionally requires vasopressors to keep MAP ≥65 mmHg and a lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation, which he does not need because his blood pressure responds to fluid. SIRS criteria are no longer used to define sepsis, and bacteraemia is simply organisms in the blood. Management follows the sepsis bundle: cultures, antibiotics within 1 hour and fluids.

why: Stem was split across two items and lost its data; rebuilt as one question with the source values and Sepsis-3 discriminators; key (sepsis) from the source; replaced the meaningless 'possibly harmful systemic response' option

set.stem: A 68-year-old man with previous splenectomy is in septic shock with no clear source. Local rates of cephalosporin-resistant Streptococcus pneumoniae exceed 1%. Which empirical regimen is most appropriate?
set.explanation: Asplenic patients are at risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection, mainly from encapsulated organisms, with S. pneumoniae the commonest; a third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime or ceftriaxone) covers pneumococcus, meningococcus and H. influenzae, and vancomycin is added where cephalosporin-resistant pneumococci are prevalent. Vancomycin alone misses Gram-negatives, and quinolone regimens are less reliable for these organisms in septic shock. Prevention is by vaccination, prophylactic penicillin and a standby course of antibiotics.

set.stem: All of the following therapies initially looked promising but have not improved mortality in sepsis EXCEPT:
options: Red cell transfusion only when haemoglobin falls below 70 g/L
Intensive insulin therapy for tight glucose control
ACTH stimulation testing to select patients for steroid therapy
set.explanation: A restrictive transfusion threshold (haemoglobin 70 g/L) is as safe as, or better than, a liberal strategy in septic and critically ill patients (TRICC and TRISS trials) and is standard practice. Activated protein C was withdrawn after PROWESS-SHOCK showed no benefit, tight glucose control increased mortality in NICE-SUGAR, tissue factor pathway inhibitor failed, and ACTH testing does not identify who benefits from hydrocortisone, which is now given on clinical grounds to patients with refractory shock.

set.stem: A 62-year-old man with an acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction (ECG shown) develops cardiogenic shock while being prepared for primary PCI: BP 78/50 mmHg, cool peripheries, clear lung fields and a lactate of 4.5 mmol/L. Which agent is most appropriate first to support his blood pressure?
set.explanation: In cardiogenic shock complicating MI the priority is urgent revascularisation (primary PCI of the culprit lesion), with noradrenaline as the first-line vasopressor to restore perfusion pressure because it caused fewer arrhythmias and deaths than dopamine (SOAP II); dobutamine may be added for low output. Routine intra-aortic balloon pumping is no longer recommended after IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit, and VA-ECMO is reserved for refractory shock. Nitrates and diuretics lower blood pressure further, and vasopressin is a second-line vasopressor.

why: Source key (intra-aortic balloon pump) is outdated: IABP-SHOCK II and ESC guidance advise against routine IABP; question rebuilt around first-line vasopressor (noradrenaline); moved to Mixed Cardiology

set.stem: A 72-year-old man with known ischaemic cardiomyopathy (EF 20%) presents in cardiogenic shock with pulmonary oedema: BP 82/50 mmHg, cool extremities, SpO2 84% despite high-flow oxygen and a respiratory rate of 34/min. All of the following are appropriate EXCEPT:
options: Furosemide 60 mg IV once perfusion pressure is supported
set.explanation: Morphine is no longer recommended routinely in acute heart failure: it causes vasodilatation and hypotension, respiratory depression and nausea, and registry data link it to more ventilation and higher mortality, so it is especially hazardous in shock. Noradrenaline to restore perfusion pressure, dobutamine to increase contractility, a loop diuretic for congestion once blood pressure is supported, and ventilatory support for refractory hypoxaemia are all appropriate. The cause of decompensation (ischaemia, arrhythmia, infection) must be sought and treated.

set.stem: A 52-year-old man develops acute pulmonary oedema and hypotension 4 days after an inferior myocardial infarction, with a new apical systolic murmur; acute severe mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture is suspected. What would a pulmonary artery catheter most likely show?
set.explanation: In acute severe mitral regurgitation the regurgitant jet enters a small, non-compliant left atrium, producing a raised pulmonary capillary wedge pressure with giant v waves during ventricular systole, together with low forward cardiac output. Equalisation of diastolic pressures is the pattern of tamponade, a high RA pressure with low wedge suggests RV infarction, and a high cardiac output with low wedge pressure is seen in early sepsis. Management is afterload reduction and urgent surgical repair; a step-up in oxygen saturation in the RV would instead point to ventricular septal rupture.

why: Removed attached haemodynamic table image, which did not match the text options; stem expanded to a self-contained vignette; moved to Mixed Cardiology

set.stem: All of the following statements about sudden cardiac death (SCD) are true EXCEPT:
options: Coronary artery disease is the commonest underlying substrate in adults
In about two-thirds of cases SCD is the first manifestation of heart disease or occurs in patients previously thought to be at low risk
Asystole and pulseless electrical activity are commonly encountered initial rhythms in SCD arrests
A parental history of SCD increases the risk in offspring
Most victims have a previously documented left ventricular ejection fraction of 35% or less
set.explanation: Although an EF ≤35% is the main criterion for a primary-prevention ICD, most sudden cardiac deaths occur in people with no known heart disease or with only moderately reduced or normal EF, which is why SCD is often the first event. Coronary disease underlies about 80% of adult cases, VF remains important but asystole and PEA are increasingly common initial rhythms, and a parental history of SCD roughly doubles an offspring's risk. Rates are also higher in men and in Black populations.

why: Original EXCEPT key rested on a disputed definitional point that its own explanation affirmed; rewritten so exactly one statement is false (most victims do not have a known EF ≤35%); moved to Mixed Cardiology

set.stem: Which of the following conditions can produce true coma, rather than being a state that mimics coma?
set.explanation: Coma is a state of unarousable unresponsiveness with eyes closed, produced by bilateral hemispheric dysfunction or damage to the brainstem reticular activating system, and diffuse metabolic encephalopathy (hypoglycaemia, uraemia, hepatic failure, hyponatraemia, drugs) is among its commonest causes. The vegetative state has sleep–wake cycles with eyes open, akinetic mutism and catatonia are awake but unresponsive states, and the locked-in patient is fully conscious and can communicate with vertical eye movements. Recognising these mimics prevents misdiagnosis.

why: Stem ('which state correctly identifies a patient in a coma') was ambiguous; reworded so the keyed answer is clearly the only cause of true coma

set.stem: A 74-year-old man has a large subdural haematoma with uncal herniation (MRI shown). What is the cause of his coma?
options: Compression of the anterior and posterior cerebral arteries
Compression of the midbrain against the opposite tentorial edge
Compression of the opposite cerebral peduncle
Downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils into the foramen magnum
Entrapment of the ventricles causing hydrocephalus
set.explanation: When the medial temporal lobe (uncus) herniates across the tentorium it compresses the ipsilateral third nerve (dilated pupil) and pushes the midbrain against the opposite tentorial edge; distortion of the midbrain reticular activating system produces coma. Pressure on the opposite cerebral peduncle gives the Kernohan notch phenomenon (hemiparesis ipsilateral to the mass) but not coma itself, and compression of the posterior cerebral artery causes occipital infarction. Tonsillar herniation compresses the medulla, causing respiratory arrest.

set.stem: A 44-year-old man is found comatose, flushed, with 5 mm pupils, muscle spasms and rapid breathing. What is the most likely cause of his coma?
set.explanation: Coma without focal neurological signs, with flushing, preserved pupillary size and reactivity, myoclonic or muscle twitching and hyperventilation, points to a toxic or metabolic cause, most often drug intoxication (for example anticholinergic, tricyclic or salicylate poisoning). Concussion causes only brief loss of consciousness, cortical vein thrombosis produces seizures and focal signs, and meningitis or systemic infection would usually cause fever and neck stiffness. A toxicology screen, glucose, electrolytes and ABG should be obtained.

set.stem: In which patient is intraparenchymal intracranial pressure monitoring preferred over a ventriculostomy?
options: A 24-year-old with traumatic brain injury and GCS 6
A 35-year-old with fulminant hepatic failure and INR 3.5
A 48-year-old man with subarachnoid haemorrhage and hydrocephalus
A 68-year-old with a large haemorrhagic stroke and midline shift
set.explanation: A ventriculostomy (external ventricular drain) measures ICP and also allows CSF drainage, so it is preferred in TBI, SAH with hydrocephalus and intracerebral haemorrhage, but it carries a higher bleeding risk. In fulminant hepatic failure with coagulopathy, a less invasive intraparenchymal fibre-optic monitor is used (after correcting coagulopathy where possible) to guide treatment of cerebral oedema. The other patients benefit from the therapeutic drainage a ventriculostomy provides.

set.stem: A 56-year-old woman with subarachnoid haemorrhage has an external ventricular drain in place, and her intracranial pressure rises to 45 mmHg. What is the next management step?
options: No action, as cerebral perfusion pressure is adequate
Open the ventriculostomy to drain CSF to an ICP below 20–25 mmHg
Hyperventilate to a PaCO2 of 4 kPa (30 mmHg)
set.explanation: With a ventricular drain already in place, draining CSF is the quickest and safest first measure to lower ICP (aiming for <20–25 mmHg) because it removes volume directly. Osmotherapy with mannitol or hypertonic saline is the next step if drainage is insufficient, and brief hyperventilation is only a temporary bridge because vasoconstriction risks ischaemia. Corticosteroids do not help oedema after SAH or trauma, and an ICP of 45 mmHg is dangerous regardless of the calculated perfusion pressure.

set.stem: A 67-year-old man has been in the ICU with sepsis for 3 weeks and now cannot be weaned from the ventilator. He has symmetrical weakness of all limbs, worse distally, with absent tendon reflexes and reduced distal sensation; nerve conduction studies show an axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. What is the most likely cause?
set.explanation: Critical illness polyneuropathy is an axonal sensorimotor neuropathy complicating sepsis and multiorgan failure; it causes distal weakness, areflexia and sensory loss and involves the phrenic nerves, leading to failure to wean. Critical illness myopathy (often after corticosteroids and neuromuscular blockers) causes proximal weakness with preserved sensation and normal sensory nerve conduction. Guillain–Barré syndrome is demyelinating and starts before ICU admission, delirium does not cause weakness, and fibroproliferative ARDS would show on imaging. Management is supportive with early rehabilitation and glycaemic control.

why: Added examination and nerve conduction findings so polyneuropathy is distinguishable from critical illness myopathy

set.stem: A 56-year-old woman with a subarachnoid haemorrhage improves initially, but on day 7 has an abrupt neurological decline. CT shows no new blood. What is the most likely cause?
set.explanation: Vasospasm causing delayed cerebral ischaemia typically appears 3–14 days after aneurysmal SAH (peak days 7–10) with new focal deficits or reduced consciousness, and CT shows no new haemorrhage. Rebleeding is most frequent in the first 24 hours and would show fresh blood, hydrocephalus would show enlarged ventricles, and hyponatraemia (from cerebral salt wasting) develops more gradually. Nimodipine is given to all patients for 21 days to reduce ischaemic complications, and transcranial Doppler or CT angiography confirms spasm.

set.stem: A 56-year-old woman develops delayed neurological deterioration on day 7 after a coiled aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage. CT shows no new blood, and CT angiography confirms severe cerebral vasospasm. She is already taking nimodipine. What treatment do you recommend now?
options: IV noradrenaline to raise blood pressure and referral for balloon angioplasty
set.explanation: Symptomatic vasospasm is treated by maintaining euvolaemia and raising blood pressure with a vasopressor such as noradrenaline to improve perfusion through narrowed vessels, with endovascular balloon angioplasty or intra-arterial vasodilators for refractory or focal spasm. The aneurysm is already secured, fluid restriction worsens ischaemia (and hyponatraemia after SAH is usually salt wasting), a ventriculostomy treats hydrocephalus, and hyperventilation causes further cerebral vasoconstriction.

set.stem: A 21-year-old with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and a white cell count of 156 × 10⁹/L starts induction chemotherapy. Which is NOT a feature of tumour lysis syndrome?
set.explanation: Rapid tumour cell breakdown releases potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids (metabolised to uric acid), so hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia and hyperuricaemia occur, with acute kidney injury from urate and calcium phosphate precipitation. Calcium is bound by the excess phosphate, causing hypocalcaemia (tetany, arrhythmias), not hypercalcaemia. High-risk patients (bulky leukaemia or lymphoma, high white count) need aggressive hydration and rasburicase or allopurinol.

set.stem: All of the following are important in preventing tumour lysis syndrome EXCEPT:
options: Adequate IV hydration (about 3 L/m² per day)
Rasburicase for patients at high risk
Frequent serum biochemistry (every 4–6 hours) in high-risk patients
set.explanation: Prevention of tumour lysis syndrome relies on vigorous IV hydration to maintain a high urine output, a hypouricaemic agent (allopurinol, or rasburicase in high-risk patients or established hyperuricaemia) and close biochemical monitoring. Dialysis is reserved for established TLS with refractory hyperkalaemia, fluid overload or severe AKI and is not given prophylactically. Urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended, as it promotes calcium phosphate and xanthine precipitation.

why: Distractor 'urine alkalinisation to pH >7' is itself no longer recommended, creating a second correct answer; replaced with rasburicase for high-risk patients

set.stem: An overweight middle-aged man sees his GP after his wife complains about his loud snoring. He drinks large amounts of alcohol in the evenings before bed. Which of the following symptoms is he most likely to report?
set.explanation: Excessive daytime sleepiness from repeated arousals and fragmented sleep is the cardinal symptom of obstructive sleep apnoea, and obesity and evening alcohol (which reduces upper-airway muscle tone) both worsen airway collapse. Morning headache, nocturnal choking, reduced libido and personality change occur but are less common. Sleepiness is quantified with the Epworth scale, and he should be advised about driving, weight loss and avoiding alcohol before bed while awaiting a sleep study.

why: Same idea and level as resinf-0035 (chronic purulent cough with recurrent infections and haemoptysis in a non-smoker = bronchiectasis)

set.explanation: Continuous positive airway pressure splints the pharynx open during sleep and is the most effective treatment for symptomatic moderate-to-severe OSA, improving sleepiness, quality of life, driving safety and blood pressure. Mandibular advancement devices are an alternative for mild disease or CPAP intolerance, upper-airway surgery helps only selected patients, and modafinil treats residual sleepiness but not the apnoeas. Weight loss should be advised for everyone but rarely cures severe OSA on its own and takes time.

set.stem: In which of the following patients presenting to the emergency department with acute dyspnoea would a positive D-dimer result prompt further testing for pulmonary embolism?
options: A 24-year-old woman who is 32 weeks pregnant
A 48-year-old man with no past medical history who has calf pain after prolonged air travel and a normal alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient
A 56-year-old woman receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer
A 62-year-old man who had hip replacement surgery 4 weeks ago
A 72-year-old man who had an acute myocardial infarction 2 weeks ago
set.explanation: D-dimer is sensitive but non-specific: it is useful only in outpatients with low or intermediate pre-test probability, in whom a negative result excludes PE and a positive one leads to CTPA. It is raised anyway in pregnancy, cancer, recent surgery and recent MI, so in those patients a positive test adds nothing and they should proceed straight to imaging if PE is suspected. A normal A–a gradient does not exclude PE, so the otherwise well traveller with calf pain is the patient in whom a positive D-dimer is meaningful.

set.stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with acute breathlessness 2 days after developing calf pain and swelling following a 9-hour car journey. BP 98/60 mmHg, HR 114/min, RR 28/min, SpO2 92% on room air, weight 89 kg; the lungs are clear and the right leg is swollen and tender. ABG: pH 7.52, PaCO2 3.3 kPa (25 mmHg), PaO2 9.1 kPa (68 mmHg). Kidney and liver function are normal, and CT confirms pulmonary embolism. All of the following agents can be used alone as initial therapy EXCEPT:
set.explanation: Warfarin takes 5–7 days to become effective and initially lowers protein C (a transient prothrombotic state), so it must be overlapped with a parenteral anticoagulant for at least 5 days and until the INR is ≥2 for 24 hours. LMWH (enoxaparin or tinzaparin), fondaparinux and IV unfractionated heparin are all effective immediate treatments, and apixaban or rivaroxaban can also be started alone as oral monotherapy. This patient is normotensive, so thrombolysis is not indicated.

Acute PE causes alveolar hyperventilation, driven by reflex stimulation of pulmonary receptors and hypoxaemia, giving hypocapnia and respiratory alkalosis. Airway resistance increases (bronchoconstriction) rather than decreases, and DVT is found at presentation in only about half of patients. Hypotension results from right ventricular failure with septal shift reducing LV filling, not primary LV systolic dysfunction, and the A–a gradient correlates poorly with clot size and can be normal.

set.stem: A 57-year-old man with hypertension is admitted with pulmonary embolism. BP 132/62 mmHg, HR 85/min, SpO2 95% on room air; echocardiography shows normal right heart size and function and troponin is undetectable. Doppler shows extensive femoral–popliteal DVT. He is started on LMWH with warfarin and asks whether he should have an inferior vena cava (IVC) filter. What is the most appropriate answer?
set.explanation: An IVC filter is indicated only when anticoagulation is contraindicated (e.g. active bleeding) or has failed (recurrent PE despite therapeutic anticoagulation); this low-risk patient can be anticoagulated and would not benefit. Filters do not improve survival, increase later DVT and can thrombose or migrate, and a retrievable device should be removed as soon as anticoagulation is possible. Residual leg thrombus, clot burden, age or sex are not indications on their own, although there are defined indications, so the statement that none exist is wrong.
